phase1.intro:
FileReader and FileWriter work fine, but every single read() or write() call can mean an actual trip to the disk. Buffered streams fix this.

Where should we start?

dialogue: [[term:BufferedReader]] wraps an existing Reader — `new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"))` — and reads big chunks into an in-memory buffer, so most read() calls just pull from memory instead of hitting the disk again.
It also hands you `readLine()`, a genuinely convenient method the raw FileReader never had.

stickyNote.definition: BufferedReader wraps a Reader, buffering reads into memory to reduce disk trips, and adds readLine() for reading a full line at once.

dialogue: [[term:BufferedWriter]] collects your writes in memory and flushes them to disk in bigger batches, plus gives you `newLine()`.

[[key:Wrapping one stream inside another to add functionality]] is a pattern worth recognizing on its own — BufferedReader doesn't replace FileReader, it wraps it, adding buffering and readLine() on top.

stickyNote.flavor: 🎁 wrapping a stream to add functionality on top
stickyNote.definition: BufferedWriter batches writes and adds newLine(). Buffered streams follow a wrap-to-extend pattern seen throughout Java's I/O classes.

topics.buttonText: Why does readLine() return null instead of an empty string?
dialogue: [[warn:readLine() returns null, specifically, when it hits the end of the file]] — not an empty string, null. [[key:That's why every BufferedReader reading loop checks for null]]: `while ((line = br.readLine()) != null)`.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚫 null means end of file, not empty string
stickyNote.definition: readLine() returns null (not an empty string) at end of file — reading loops must check for null, not for empty content.

phase2.errorMessage:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "line" is null
    at Test.main(Test.java:9)
phase2.explanation:
This loop never checks whether readLine() returned null — it just keeps calling it forever, assuming there's always another line. The moment the file actually runs out, readLine() returns null, and the loop tries to use that null value as if it were a real line, which is exactly where the NullPointerException comes from.

[[warn:this is genuinely THE most common BufferedReader mistake]] — it's easy to write while (true) { line = br.readLine(); ... } out of habit and forget that readLine() is the thing telling you when to stop.

[[key:the fix folds the null-check directly into the loop condition]]: while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) { System.out.println(line); } — the loop naturally ends the moment there's nothing left to read, no separate check needed.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a loop forgets to check for null~

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's wrap a stream for speed and convenience~

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Uses BufferedWriter to write 5 lines to a file called "poem.txt"
2. Lines: any 5 lines of your choice
3. Uses BufferedReader to read the file back
4. Prints each line with a line number prefix: "1: [line]"

Use try-with-resources for both operations.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the performance gap buffering closes is real and significant — reading a file one byte at a time can mean one system call to the OS per byte, while a BufferedReader typically fetches several kilobytes per actual disk read. For a large file, that difference alone can be the gap between a program finishing in milliseconds versus taking seconds.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
